c.v: What C++11 guarantees: if two threads reach

at the same moment, exactly one of them runs the constructor, the other waits for it to finish, and both go on to see the same fully built object. What it does not cover is anything past that point. Calling

You pass if the identity check compares references with

Getting the identity right without saying where the guarantee stops is a partial pass. Saying the finished object is now safe to call from several threads is a fail: that is exactly the mistake the guarantee invites.

Singleton is a creational pattern that promises a class exactly one instance, reached through one point of access that anyone in the program can call, rather than a reference passed to whoever needs it. In C++ its usual shape is a private constructor and a static member function returning a reference to a function-local static object of the class: the
, after Scott Meyers, who proposed it as the fix for a different problem, the order in which ordinary global objects in separate files get built.
Naming it a pattern is generous. The problem it is reached for, exactly one shared instance the whole program can see, already has an honest fix: build the object once, in

or in whatever owns it, and pass a reference to whoever needs it. A Singleton skips that fix and puts the instance behind a function name instead of a parameter, so a class that needs it does not receive it from its caller: it reaches into the function and takes it.

The mechanism does get one thing right. C++11 guarantees that the first construction of a function-local static is thread-safe even when two threads call the function at the same moment, one building it while the other waits, with a hidden guard that makes every later call cheap. That guarantee stops at construction. It says nothing about calling the object's own methods from two threads afterward, and it removes neither of the pattern's real costs: a class that reaches for a Singleton hides that dependency from its own constructor, so no test can hand it a fake, and the object is torn down, at program exit, in the reverse order of when it was first used, an order a second Singleton's destructor can outlive by one line in

You meet a genuine need for exactly one instance in a small number of places the language itself forces: a signal handler's flag, whose fixed signature has no room for a captured object, and the counter inside a replacement
. Everywhere else, and in this interview, the honest answer passes the instance in.

starts and never again after. That order of calls, not a fixed position in the file, is what makes the object lazy. The reference

Laziness is not the whole guarantee. Before C++11, two threads reaching
at once could both see an uninitialised guard and both start building

, a plain race. The 2011 standard closed it, and cppreference states the fix directly: if multiple threads attempt to initialise the same function-local static concurrently, the initialisation occurs exactly once, and usual implementations reduce the cost of every later call to a single non-atomic boolean check once the object exists. Read that sentence for what it leaves out. It covers the one call that builds
, or any method the finished object exposes afterward, and nothing in the standard extends the same protection there. Two threads calling a method that mutates

once it exists still race exactly as they would on any other shared object with no lock of its own: the guard C++11 added protects the moment of construction, not the object's whole lifetime. The chapter on mutexes later in this course is where that gap actually closes, with a lock the class owns for itself.
Scott Meyers proposed the function-local static in

, Item 4, not as a pattern to reach for on purpose but as the fix for a narrower problem: two ordinary global objects in separate translation units, one needed by the other during its own construction, with no rule in the standard for which file's globals run first. Moving each into its own function-local static sidesteps the question, because a function-local static builds on first use, and first use has a definite order that the program's own control flow decides rather than the linker. Reused as a Singleton, the same mechanism fixes that ordering question and opens two new ones, worked through below: everyone who calls

now shares one object with no say in when it appears, and, as the failure cases below show, no say in when it disappears either. A finished Singleton class also deletes its copy and move operations the way this course's other polymorphic bases do, because nothing about a function-local static stops
from building a second, fully working instance, which would make "exactly one" a claim the compiler never checks.

c.v: The Factory Method topic's worked example used the other forced case for real, a counter inside a replacement
, whose signature is equally fixed and equally unable to take the counter as an argument. Core Guidelines

names global mutable state as something to avoid, and both of these are its stated exceptions, not a licence to reach for a third one. Neither is a Singleton class with a getter; both are a plain variable at namespace scope, used exactly where the language leaves no other place to put it.
Everywhere else, the same shape hides a dependency instead of forcing one. A function that calls
inside its own body takes no

parameter, so its signature promises less than it needs: the dependency injection topic named this as the first roadblock to testing anything, a class that builds or reaches for what it depends on instead of receiving it. A test that wants a different
cannot hand one to the function; it can only mutate the one

every other test shares, which is the exact bug the factory method topic measured in a registry: one test's change to shared state outlives that test and reaches the next one, in whichever order the test runner happens to pick.
The third cost is destruction order, and it takes real code to see it, not a description alone.
's destructor writes one last line through
, on the heap buffer that used to hold
's name. The standard destroys function-local statics in the reverse order of when their construction finished, and that order is exactly the order
that no longer exists. Nothing about this needs two threads or an unlucky race. It is entirely deterministic, and it is exactly as fragile as the two lines in
that decided the order, which a change to some unrelated piece of start-up code, months later, can silently reverse.

Every one of these three costs comes from the same source: a Singleton is reachable from anywhere, so nothing about where it is used tells you what depends on it, in what order it was built, or whether a test changed it under you. Global coupling is the name for that property, not an extra fourth cost, and it is why Klaus Iglberger's Guidelines 37 and 38 in C++ Software Design treat Singleton as an implementation detail at best: if a process genuinely needs exactly one instance of something, put an interface in front of it and inject that one instance everywhere it is used, the same constructor injection the dependency injection topic already gave you, so a test can inject a different one instead of fighting the real one for control of a shared global. Pete Muldoon's CppCon talk on retiring the pattern makes the same case from the other side: nearly every reason code reaches for a Singleton is better served by building the object once, where the program starts, and passing it down.
